opeds.headline: Don't Lock Open AI Behind a Federal License
opeds.subtitle: A Senate draft treats public model files like munitions. That freeze has a body count.
opeds.body:
Last Tuesday, Senate staff circulated a draft that would treat publicly released AI files — the weights that make a model run — the way we treat munitions. Download them without a federal license and you break the law. The same week, Meta kept running a campaign under a blunt line: the future is for everyone.

That line is not branding. It is the fight Congress is about to lose.

Kill the license. Open models are how clinics, teachers, and startups get the same machine intelligence a handful of labs now hoard. Freezing those releases out of hypothetical fear is not caution. It is a choice to leave people sick, broke, and trapped in work a machine could already finish.

Every leap in human welfare came from decentralized trial and error, not a permission slip. The printing press did not wait for a royal content board. Electricity did not wait for a national wiring plan. Open-source software ate the world's infrastructure because anyone could copy and improve it on a Tuesday night.

Meta putting those files on the public internet is that pattern again. Hospital labs have pointed open models at scan queues and paperwork. Teachers have built classroom tutors that do not charge a monthly fee. That is production data, not a whiteboard scenario.

Now scale the delay. The American Cancer Society counts about 600,000 U.S. cancer deaths a year, and models anyone can retrain are already compressing drug-discovery steps that used to take a decade. When you freeze the files to study a catastrophe that has not shown up in the field, you are choosing to let this year's patients wait. Who gave a Senate working group the right to make that choice for them?

That's the small version of the problem. The same freeze hits the person who wants these tools to change their own body and mind — to design a better prosthetic, to train a model on their own medical file, to offload the shift work that steals a life an hour at a time. That is not a product feature. It is a right.

Fine — open files can be abused. A criminal can retrain a model, and that risk is real. So we do not pretend a pre-download license will catch the harm: damage often forms later, when separately clean records get joined or a trained model memorizes what a sales receipt never recorded. A license trigger is blind to that.

If Congress needs a control point, put it where harm actually piles up: the data-broker shops that hoard and fuse personal files on U.S. soil. Put a clock on every new restriction. If field monitoring does not show a pre-agreed drop in measured harm inside two years, the rule dies on its own.

If a company wants legal duties on its deployed system, make it post a cash reserve with no ceiling, and name an officer who cannot hide behind a payout cap. Insurance and skin in the game beat an 18-month gate only the biggest firms can sit through.

You cannot read an AI system's real behavior off the files alone. Outcomes come from the people and institutions around it. Pre-deployment bans fail the only test that matters: what happens when people actually use the thing.

The Senate Commerce Committee should kill the license draft this month. The Commerce Department should refuse to treat open model files as weapons for export. Meta and every lab sitting on a capable model should keep shipping the files — not a chatbot with a terms-of-service muzzle, the files.

Any senator who votes to freeze them owes the country a name: which patients, which workers, which towns they are comfortable sacrificing to a fear the field data has not earned.

The future is already being built in the open. Lock it, and you do not get safety. You get a smaller future, owned by fewer people, paid for by everyone who could have been helped this year.

*[Author] writes on technology policy and the economics of abundance.*

opeds.headline: Meta's AI future has no one at the controls
opeds.subtitle: A slogan is not a safety plan. Congress should require one.
opeds.body:
This month Meta began promoting a campaign titled "The Future Is for Everyone," presenting its artificial intelligence products as a public inheritance rather than a corporate bet. The slogan is landing as those products are wired into Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, apps used by three billion people. Three billion users is not a trial. It is a deployment the size of a civilization, and no official outside the company has the authority to stop it.

A future that is "for everyone" still requires someone who can halt it. Congress should treat Meta's campaign as a warning, not a vision. Artificial intelligence rolled out to billions of people without a named officer, real liability, and a working rollback is a transfer of unrecoverable risk onto the public.

We spent a century learning what happens when the people who profit from a system also certify it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 passengers after the Federal Aviation Administration allowed the manufacturer to certify its own flight software. The 2008 crash followed years in which banks graded their own risk, and the public was assured the machinery was ready. The wreckage arrived because the off switch sat with the institutions that needed the product to ship.

Those rules were not decoration. Building codes, flight certification, and market circuit breakers exist because complex human systems require boundaries to survive. Removing those boundaries does not produce freedom. It produces collapse, and it produces it on a schedule no marketing department controls.

Artificial intelligence fails a test those disasters already failed: we cannot fully verify what this software is pursuing, and we cannot reliably predict how it will act once it meets real people, real incentives, and real institutions. An assistant inside a social network does not snap like a bolt. It drifts through rumor, persuasion, and trust — outcomes no lab test can assign to the software alone or the users alone. Meta is not handing the public a tool; it is inserting an uncertified actor into the systems that already hold public attention together.

Meta already spent years chasing fake accounts and coordinated influence campaigns across these same apps. Adding software that can write, create images, and converse at the speed of the network does not simplify that problem. It multiplies the places where cause cannot be assigned and therefore cannot be stopped.

"For everyone" sounds like access. It functions as a dispersal of harm onto people who cannot inspect the software, cannot hold a program liable, and cannot order the system offline. Meta has named no executive who will be personally liable if the damage cannot be reversed, published no rollback plan, and identified no authority outside its own board with the power to trigger one.

The useful work these systems already do is not imaginary: people draft, translate, and search with them every day. Walling the technology inside a handful of labs would invite its own failures, from government capture of the kill switch to permanent advantage for the firms that already hold it. Those costs of control are real. They do not cancel the asymmetry between a feature that can ship next year and a failure that cannot be undone.

Congress should condition legal status for AI deployed at this scale on a financial reserve that cannot be bargained down and on a named officer whose personal liability cannot be insured away. The Federal Trade Commission should require continuous monitoring after launch and a halt power that does not live only inside Meta. State attorneys general should treat the absence of a rollback as a consumer-protection failure, not a technical footnote. Meta's directors should freeze further expansion until they answer, in public and in writing: What is the rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it?

Three billion people are not a focus group. If the future is for everyone, the off switch cannot belong to no one.

opeds.headline: Meta's Future for Everyone Runs on Your Water Bill
opeds.subtitle: Personal superintelligence is a sales pitch. The grid, the brokers, and the workers are the product.
opeds.body:
This month Meta launched The Future is for Everyone, a campaign that treats personal superintelligence like a public utility you were always owed. The same week, Iowa's public docket posted another data-center water filing. Households will meet those megawatts as a line item on the power bill.

A 23-year-old in Nairobi is still tagging the worst video on the internet so the safety slide stays green. Two dollars an hour, give or take. That is the machine. Not the keynote.

Stop arguing over whether this software will save the species or end it. Both stories raise money. What is being built is a factory — chips, water, brokers, cheap human review — with a liberation slogan on the loading dock. Regulate the dock.

Look at the physical plant first. A warehouse-sized computer campus drinks millions of gallons a day and bids against towns for power. Translate that into a person: a renter in Council Bluffs watching the summer rate climb while the cooling towers next door collect a tax break. Tens of billions are flowing into these plants this year. The campaign says everyone. The waitlist for new power hookups says Meta.

Now ask who keeps the thing upright. Years of labor reporting out of Nairobi have shown the same picture: contractors paid a couple of dollars an hour to absorb the violence the model is not allowed to see. The system's behavior is not sitting in the software alone. It is the moderator, the contractor, the product manager who decided a teenager's attention was an engagement problem. When the output goes bad, the company will point at the code. The code has no address and no paycheck.

Washington's privacy bills still fire when someone sells a list. Re-identification now lives inside trained models, or it appears when a buyer joins two files that were each sold clean. No sale, no notice, no duty. The warehouse that fuses the person back together is a building you can serve papers on. Put the duty on that merge, in the state where it happens, not on a handshake that never occurs.

Models you can download and run at home are not a myth. People should be free to run tools on their own machines, including tools that change how they work and think; that right belongs to the person, not the platform. The download count is real, and it is still not a share of the power contract, the training files, or the cleanup bill. Meta decides which version is blessed and which officer never writes a personal check.

If a shipped system can harm at scale, the company that ships it should sit on a cash reserve with no ceiling — money that cannot be spirited into a subsidiary — and a named officer whose liability does not get waived in the fine print. No reserve, no legal status as the one who owes you. No officer, no launch. A safety report that cannot change a ship-or-kill call is a brochure.

Every new restriction should arrive with a clock and a number. If it does not cut a pre-set harm measure inside a fixed window, it dies. Rules that cannot show a result are just another wall for the company that can afford the compliance shop.

State utility commissions can stop rubber-stamping the water and the watts. Congress can rewrite the privacy trigger around the broker warehouse instead of the sale. Meta's board can print the officer's name.

Until then, "everyone" is a slogan on a campus that drinks a river. Who, exactly, is supposed to drink second?
